I’m looking for my next role: designing and building websites, leading the team that does, or sales and solutions engineering in the web space.

The site I’m proudest of is Quantum Home Cares. They came to me as a referral after a previous web designer burned them and even held their domain and website hostage, so earning their trust took time. Now other companies in their industry compliment them on the site, and the form fills and sign-ups keep coming in.

My hardest technical problem: Quantum Home Cares wanted every lead from their Netlify form to get a yes or no click, and every yes to land automatically as a lead in their industry CRM. Figuring out the API keys and automation took a while, with Resend in the mix, but it ended up working perfectly.

Every project starts with a discovery call. I figure out what the business is struggling with and what the site is actually for. Usually that’s bringing in business, but sometimes it’s informational, like explaining their process or standards. Then I learn what makes them stand out.
I build the homepage first to lock in a design direction the client loves, then the inside pages, then feedback rounds until launch.

I skip Figma most of the time and go straight into code. I can picture the page flow in my head, and with the components and processes I’ve built over the years, I can code a homepage faster than I could mock it up.

When a client hates a design, it’s usually not hate. They just didn’t know what they wanted until they saw it. So I find out exactly what isn’t working, go back through discovery with site inspiration and examples, learn what they like about each, and start fresh.

Accessibility and performance are the most important parts of a website. They separate someone who can design from someone who actually understands the web. Restaurants get sued over even minor accessibility issues, so at BentoBox they were at the front of everything we did, and I always spend real time on QA before a launch.

These days my least favorite platform is WordPress, especially with page builders like Divi. Webflow and Framer are top tier, Wix and Squarespace are mid-tier, and my favorite is still hand-coding in Astro.

I love design, but I understand software, websites and technology even more, and I love talking about them. When I get excited about something, I want to teach it and get other people excited too. At BentoBox I went from designing all day to handling more and more client calls, and found I love getting clients excited about the platform and how to get the most out of it.
I explain technical things the way Oscar explained a surplus to Michael Scott: like you’re five, with an analogy to something everyday so it sticks.

At BentoBox, Bar Saikindo handed us a mockup from an outside design team that was built for print, not the web. One page was a fully working DJ turntable. I talked them out of the turntable, used their assets as a jumping-off point, and built a site that works on every screen size and that they’re really excited about.

The product I’d most love to demo is a platform built for one industry, the way BentoBox is for restaurants. Learning what makes it special for that industry is exciting, and it’s easy to sell when the features live up to the hype.

My team would call me efficient and a teacher. When a designer had a video that wouldn’t load or size right, I didn’t just hand over the fix. I walked them through why it broke and why the new code works. I’d rather teach someone to fix it than give them a snippet.
I’m quick once I’m in a focus zone, and I’m a stickler on QA. I’ll spend the extra time making padding, spacing and font sizes consistent across every component and screen size.

In a design review I look for consistent spacing, type and color, and a clear flow of information. Sections should flow naturally into each other with no harsh edges. Then accessibility: alt text on every image and colors that meet the 4.5:1 contrast ratio.

The mindset I push on my team: there’s almost always a solution. A platform limitation doesn’t mean you’re stuck. JavaScript usually finds a way, and you can bounce ideas off each other or use AI to dig into what’s blocking you.

My ideal next role is customer-facing: sales or solutions engineering, showing off a product. I could also see myself leading a team at an agency and jumping on calls to put out fires. As long as it’s websites, whether designing, coding or solving problems with AI, I’m in my happy place.
I’d prefer fully remote, but I’m open to hybrid or in-office if the commute is reasonable. I’m happy to travel now and then for a remote role.
